analysis.investment_thesis: Indigo Paints has a nearly debt-free balance sheet (D/E 0.02) and decent ROCE of 19.5%, qualities I deeply respect — but at 26.9x earnings with visible growth deceleration in FY25 and FCF yield of barely 1.75%, the price demands too much optimism. I would wait for a meaningful correction before committing capital.
key_strengths: Fortress balance sheet — borrowings of just INR 24 Cr against equity of INR 1,067 Cr; D/E of 0.02 is exceptional
ROCE of 19.5% and operating margins of ~14.9% are consistent and within my preferred range, signaling a real business with pricing power in niches like roof paints and floor coatings
Revenue CAGR of 14.2% over 3 years is exactly the steady, predictable growth I look for — not explosive, not volatile
key_risks: Intense competition from Asian Paints, Berger, and Nerolac — all with far larger distribution networks, brand recall, and tinting machine penetration; Indigo is a distant challenger at INR 1,341 Cr revenue
Growth stalled in FY25 — revenue grew only 2.7% (1,306→1,341 Cr) and net profit actually declined from INR 149 Cr to INR 142 Cr; EBITDA also dipped marginally
FCF yield of ~1.75% (INR 70 Cr FCF / INR 3,995 Cr market cap) is far below my 5% threshold; heavy capex cycle restarted with CWIP jumping back to INR 221 Cr in FY25
red_flags: No dividend paid — for a profitable, cash-generating business this signals either reinvestment discipline OR promoter reluctance to share gains; I prefer the former but want confirmation
Promoter holding at 53.88% is marginally below my 55% floor — not alarming but worth watching for any further dilution
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Indigo Paints is fundamentally a well-run, conservative small-cap in decorative paints — a sector I understand well given DMart's own dealings with consumer goods. The near-zero debt (INR 27 Cr total debt vs INR 1,067 Cr equity) is the kind of balance sheet discipline I look for as the first filter. ROCE of 19.5% and operating margins holding at ~14.9% confirm this is not a commodity business — it has differentiated niches like leakproof emulsions, tile paints, and metallic finishes that allow some pricing power. The 3-year revenue CAGR of 14.2% and OCF positive in all 4 years inspires confidence in the underlying cash generation.

However, I cannot ignore the price. At 26.9x earnings, the market is pricing in sustained double-digit growth — but FY25 tells a different story: revenue grew a mere 2.7%, net profit fell INR 7 Cr, and EBITDA dipped slightly. The business hit a speed bump right as capex restarted (CWIP up from INR 17 Cr to INR 221 Cr). Competing against Asian Paints or Berger for shelf space and dealer loyalty is a war of attrition that requires massive sustained investment. At INR 838 with a FCF yield of ~1.75%, I am being asked to pay a full price for a business still proving its competitive staying power. A good business — but not at today's price.
